prompt:
Decide if

1. $\mathbb Q[x]/(x^2-1)\simeq\mathbb Q[x]/(x^2-4)$,
2. $\mathbb Q[x]/(x^2+1)\simeq\mathbb Q[x]/(x^2+2x+2)$,

where $\mathbb Q[x]$ is the ring of polynomials with rational coefficients and $(f(x))$ is the ideal in $\mathbb Q[x]$ generated by $f(x)$.

solutions.title: Change of variable
solutions.body:
For $c\in\mathbb Q\setminus\{0\}$ and $d\in\mathbb Q$, the substitution $\sigma(f)(x)=f(cx+d)$ is a ring automorphism of $\mathbb Q[x]$ (its inverse is $f(x)\mapsto f\big(\frac{x-d}{c}\big)$). It maps the ideal $(g)$ onto the ideal $(\sigma(g))$, hence induces an isomorphism $\mathbb Q[x]/(g)\cong\mathbb Q[x]/(\sigma(g))$. Multiplying the generator of an ideal by a nonzero constant does not change the ideal.

1. With $\sigma(f)(x)=f(x/2)$: $\sigma(x^2-1)=\frac{x^2}4-1=\frac14(x^2-4)$, so $\sigma\big((x^2-1)\big)=(x^2-4)$ and
$$\mathbb Q[x]/(x^2-1)\cong\mathbb Q[x]/(x^2-4).$$
2. With $\sigma(f)(x)=f(x+1)$: $\sigma(x^2+1)=(x+1)^2+1=x^2+2x+2$, so
$$\mathbb Q[x]/(x^2+1)\cong\mathbb Q[x]/(x^2+2x+2).$$

**Answer: yes in both cases.** ∎

solutions.title: Identify the rings
solutions.body:
1. $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$ with coprime factors, so by the Chinese remainder theorem the map $f\mapsto(f(1),f(-1))$ induces an isomorphism $\mathbb Q[x]/(x^2-1)\cong\mathbb Q\times\mathbb Q$. (Its kernel is the set of $f$ divisible by both $x-1$ and $x+1$, i.e. by $x^2-1$; it is onto since $(a,b)$ is the image of $\frac{a}{2}(x+1)-\frac b2(x-1)$.) In the same way $f\mapsto(f(2),f(-2))$ gives $\mathbb Q[x]/(x^2-4)\cong\mathbb Q\times\mathbb Q$. So both rings are isomorphic to $\mathbb Q\times\mathbb Q$.
2. $x^2+1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$, and $f\mapsto f(i)$ gives $\mathbb Q[x]/(x^2+1)\cong\mathbb Q(i)$. The roots of $x^2+2x+2$ are $-1\pm i$, and $f\mapsto f(-1+i)$ gives $\mathbb Q[x]/(x^2+2x+2)\cong\mathbb Q(-1+i)=\mathbb Q(i)$. So both are isomorphic to the field $\mathbb Q(i)$.

**Answer: yes, yes.**

prompt:
Let $n\ge1$ and let $m_i$ be natural numbers such that $m_i<p_{n-i}$ $(0\le i\le n-1)$, where $p_k$ is the $k$th prime. Prove that if
$$\frac{m_0}{p_n}+\frac{m_1}{p_{n-1}}+\dots+\frac{m_{n-1}}{2}$$
is a natural number then $m_0=\dots=m_{n-1}=0$.
answer: Multiply by $P=p_1p_2\cdots p_n$ and reduce modulo $p_k$: all terms but one vanish, giving $p_k\mid m_{n-k}$, and $0\le m_{n-k}<p_k$ forces $m_{n-k}=0$.

solutions.title: Reduce modulo each prime
solutions.body:
Here the $m_i$ are nonnegative integers ($0$ included) and $p_1=2<p_2=3<\dots$. Write $j=n-i$, so the sum is
$$T=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{m_{n-j}}{p_j},\qquad 0\le m_{n-j}<p_j ,$$
and suppose $T$ is an integer. Let $P=p_1p_2\cdots p_n$. Then
$$PT=\sum_{j=1}^n m_{n-j}\,\frac{P}{p_j}$$
is an integer combination, and it is divisible by every $p_k$ (because $T\in\mathbb Z$ and $p_k\mid P$).

Fix $k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$. For $j\ne k$ the number $\frac P{p_j}$ contains the factor $p_k$, so modulo $p_k$:
$$0\equiv PT\equiv m_{n-k}\,\frac{P}{p_k}\pmod{p_k}.$$
The primes are distinct, so $\frac P{p_k}$ is a product of primes different from $p_k$ and is coprime to $p_k$. Hence $p_k\mid m_{n-k}$. Since $0\le m_{n-k}<p_k$, this gives $m_{n-k}=0$.

As $k$ was arbitrary, $m_0=m_1=\dots=m_{n-1}=0$. ∎

solutions.title: Induction on $n$
solutions.body:
For $n=1$: $\frac{m_0}{2}\in\mathbb Z$ with $0\le m_0<2$ gives $m_0=0$.

Suppose the claim holds for $n-1$, and let $T=\frac{m_0}{p_n}+R$ with $R=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\frac{m_{n-j}}{p_j}$. The number $R$ is a fraction whose denominator divides $Q=p_1\cdots p_{n-1}$, which is coprime to $p_n$. Multiply $T$ by $Q$: $QT=\frac{Qm_0}{p_n}+QR$ with $QR\in\mathbb Z$, so $p_n\mid Qm_0$, hence $p_n\mid m_0$ and $m_0=0$. Then $T=R$ is an integer of the same form with $n-1$ terms (with the indices shifted: $m'_i=m_{i+1}$ and $m'_i<p_{(n-1)-i}$), and the induction hypothesis gives $m_1=\dots=m_{n-1}=0$. ∎

prompt: Let $P^{(4)}(x)=x^6+x^2+1$. Prove that $P(x)$ does not have ten distinct (real) roots.
answer: By Rolle's theorem, ten distinct real roots of $P$ would give at least six real roots of $P^{(4)}$, but $x^6+x^2+1\ge1>0$ has none.

solutions.title: Rolle's theorem four times
solutions.body:
$P$ is a polynomial of degree $10$ (its fourth derivative has degree $6$). Over $\mathbb C$ it can have ten distinct roots, so the statement is about **real** roots.

**Lemma (Rolle).** If a differentiable function $g$ has $k\ge2$ distinct real zeros $r_1<\dots<r_k$, then $g'$ has at least $k-1$ distinct real zeros, one in each open interval $(r_i,r_{i+1})$ (Rolle's theorem on $[r_i,r_{i+1}]$; the intervals are disjoint, so these zeros are distinct).

Suppose $P$ had $10$ distinct real roots. Applying the lemma four times, $P'$ has at least $9$, $P''$ at least $8$, $P'''$ at least $7$ and $P^{(4)}$ at least $6$ distinct real roots. But for every real $x$,
$$P^{(4)}(x)=x^6+x^2+1\ge1>0,$$
so $P^{(4)}$ has no real root at all. This contradiction proves the claim. ∎

(The argument even shows that $P$ has at most $4$ distinct real roots: if $P$ had $5$, then $P^{(4)}$ would have a real root.)

prompt:
Prove that if $f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ fulfils the inequalities
$$f(x)\le x,\qquad f(x+y)\le f(x)+f(y)$$
for all $x,y\in\mathbb R$, then $f(x)=x$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$.
answer: $f(0)\le0$ and $f(0)\le2f(0)$ give $f(0)=0$; then $0=f(0)\le f(x)+f(-x)\le x+(-x)=0$ forces $f(x)=x$.

solutions.title: Contradiction from a strict inequality
solutions.body:
Suppose $f(x)<x$ for some $x$. Using subadditivity and $f(-x)\le-x$,
$$f(0)=f\big(x+(-x)\big)\le f(x)+f(-x)<x+(-x)=0 .$$
But then $f(x)=f(0+x)\le f(0)+f(x)<f(x)$, a contradiction. Hence $f(x)\ge x$, and together with $f(x)\le x$ we get $f(x)=x$ for all $x$. ∎

solutions.title: Compute $f(0)$ first
solutions.body:
From $f(0)\le 0$ (first inequality) and $f(0)=f(0+0)\le 2f(0)$, i.e. $f(0)\ge0$, we get $f(0)=0$. Now for any $x$,
$$0=f(0)\le f(x)+f(-x)\le x+(-x)=0,$$
so $f(x)+f(-x)=0$. Since $f(x)\le x$ and $f(-x)\le -x$ and the two sides add up to $x+(-x)$ exactly, both inequalities must be equalities: if $f(x)<x$ then $f(x)+f(-x)<x-x=0$. Hence $f(x)=x$ for all $x$. ∎
